content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a nearest neighbor constraint for unsupervised domain generalization. Compared with the original domain generalization task, unsupervised domain generalization doesn't contain the source labels and so requires the unsupervised learning manner, such as contrastive learning. Similar to the original domain generalization task, it is critical to learn the domain invariant representation for the generalization, which reduces the intra-class distance and increases the intra-domain one. Here, this paper proposes a nearest-neighbor constraint that uses the intersection of the cross-domain nearest neighbors and the in-domain nearest neighbor's cross-domain nearest neighbors to select more credible neighbors. Some experiments are conducted on the PACS and DomainNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1) Learning invariant representation is a critical problem for the data with distribution changing. 
2) The proposed method achieved a good improvement over the vanilla contrastive learning methods which don't apply the domain invariant constraints 

Weaknesses:
1) The proposed method seems to be incremental. Compared with the original domain generalization task, the key difference is only to replace the supervised learning with source data to the self-supervised contrastive learning.  
2) In the experiment, the main methods for the comparison are contrastive learning-based methods. However, it is not surprising that using the domain invariant constraints will increase the generalization ability of models. It is suggested to compare the proposed method with different domain generalization methods (e.g. change the supervised learning with source data to the self-supervised contrastive learning),  and discuss how and why existing domain generalization methods work on the unsupervised settings, such as data generalization and augmentation methods [1,2], Domain adversarial learning[3,4], Invariant risk minimization[5], causal-based methods[6] and meta-learning methods[7].
3) Proposition 3 discusses the robustness of the proposed cd2nn and the baseline and claims that the proposed one is more accurate.
However, when comparing two nearest-neighbor selection strategies, it is better to compare both the precision and recall. Here, cd2nn uses more strict constraints which increase the precision and reduce the recall. 
4) In figure 3, two examples of cd2nn are given. In the second one, cd2nn selects {6} as the nearest neighbor. However, why {6} is better than others such as 2,3,4,5,7? 

[1] Generalizing to unseen domains via adversarial data augmentation, NeurIPS2018
[2] Domain generalization with mixstyle, ICLR2021
[3] Unsupervised domain adaptation by backpropagation, ICML2015

[5] Invariant risk minimization, arxiv2019
[6]A causal view on robustness of neural networks, NeurIPS2020

content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the novelty and contribution of this paper are incremental.  It is natural to replace supervised learning with source data for self-supervised contrastive learning in the unsupervised DG setting. 

For reproducibility, I think the method is clear and easy to follow, but I don't check the details since the source code is not attached.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this paper should be further polished. More discussions and analysis are needed.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fWJs (2)
content.comment:
>Q3: Proposition 3 discusses the robustness of the proposed cd2nn and the baseline and claims that the proposed one is more accurate. However, when comparing two nearest-neighbor selection strategies, it is better to compare both the precision and recall. Here, cd2nn uses more strict constraints which increase the precision and reduce the recall.

A3: Thanks for the question. For NN selection strategies, there is always a trade-off between accuracy and recall. Here, we think accuracy is more important to mitigate the NN match noise, which may impair the learning process. Thus, we demonstrate a more accurate search strategy with theoretical proof. Besides, we empirically verify the selection ratio of our NN search strategy. As shown in the table below, our CD2NN exhibits a relatively high selection ratio.
|Pretraining epoch|1|5|10|50|100|300|600|1000| 
|-|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
|Selection ratio of our CD2NN|0.68|0.72|0.76|0.83|0.84|0.88|0.90|0.91|
|NN accuracy of our CD2NN|0.22|0.26|0.26|0.40|0.44|0.66|0.71|0.74|


>Q4: In figure 3, two examples of cd2nn are given. In the second one, cd2nn selects {6} as the nearest neighbor. However, why {6} is better than others such as 2,3,4,5,7?

A4: Figure 3 is an illustrative sample for our CD2NN. In the second one, the first criterion is not satisfied, i.e., $\mathcal{R}_1(z, Q^{cr}_z, k)=\varnothing$. So 2,3,4,5 are not selected. For the second criterion, 6 is selected since it lies in the intersection of in-domain and cross-domain NN. While a direct cross-domain NN search finds 3 as the NN, which is with the wrong label. Using our proposed CD2NN, we can search 6 as the correct NN with the same label as the query 0.

content.title: Response to Reviewer fWJs (1)
content.comment:
>Q1: The proposed method seems to be incremental. Compared with the original domain generalization task, the key difference is only to replace the supervised learning with source data to the self-supervised contrastive learning. It is natural to replace supervised learning with source data for self-supervised contrastive learning in the unsupervised DG setting.

**A1**: Firstly, we respectfully disagree that the proposed method is incremental. We believe that pushing general ideas to new specific UDG problems and making them work is novel enough, as pointed out by Reviewer 2DB3. 

While it is natural to replace supervised learning with self-supervised contrastive learning for unlabeled data, novelty is not necessarily surprising [1]. In fact, contrastive learning is employed as the basic idea to replace supervised learning in large amounts of computer vision works. Besides, it is non-trivial to extend contrastive learning to the UDG setting on multiple datasets from different distributions. Directly extending contrastive learning fails in cross-domain scenarios. In this paper, we first delve into the failure and point out that semantic connectivity is the key to UDG. Based on this analysis, we leverage strong augmentations to suppress the intra-domain connectivity and propose a novel dual nearest neighbors search strategy to find trustworthy cross domain neighbors along with in-domain neighbors to encourage intra-class connectivity. Experimentally, as shown in Table 1 and 2, our method significantly outperforms SimCLR by 23.56\% and 23.07\% on PACS and DomainNet on average, respectively. This suggests that the analysis of vanilla contrastive learning in UDG and the design of strong augmentation and our proposed dual nearest neighbors are important, and we are the first for this attempt, which shows the significance and novelty of our work. We believe our findings are insightful for future research.

[1] https://perceiving-systems.blog/en/news/novelty-in-science

>Q2: It is suggested to compare the proposed method with different domain generalization methods (e.g. change the supervised learning with source data to the self-supervised contrastive learning), and discuss how and why existing domain generalization methods work on the unsupervised settings, such as data generalization and augmentation methods [1,2], Domain adversarial learning[3,4], Invariant risk minimization[5], causal-based methods[6] and meta-learning methods[7].

**A2**: Firstly, we emphasize that training supervision (labeled data) is indispensable in existing supervised DG methods. Due to the lack of labels to control the semantic information, existing DG methods fail to work on unsupervised settings. 
- On the one hand, some methods [1,4,5,6,7] require labels $y$ in their main loss functions, which is inherently not applicable for UDG. Without labels for supervision, they cannot compute the loss functions and so fail to be trained. 
- On the other hand, some methods [2,3] can be adapted with modifications for UDG. However, without labels for supervised classification loss, they only focus on reducing domain bias, i.e., decreasing the intra-domain connectivity, and fail to increase intra-class connectivity, which is more important to learn semantic information on unlabeled data. For example, as pointed in the ablation study of [8], domain discriminator [3] has a minor impact on performance. While our method improves the performance a lot.

[1] Generalizing to unseen domains via adversarial data augmentation, NeurIPS2018. [2] Domain generalization with mixstyle, ICLR2021. [3] Unsupervised domain adaptation by backpropagation, ICML2015. [4] Domain generalization via entropy regularization, NeurIPS2020. [5] Invariant risk minimization, arxiv2019. [6] A causal view on robustness of neural networks, NeurIPS2020. [7] Metareg: Towards domain generalization using meta-regularization, NeurIPS2018. [8] Unsupervised Domain Generalization by Learning a Bridge Across Domains, CVPR2022.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper study the problem of unsupervised domain generalization (UDG) where both source and target datasets are unlabeled. Two issues with vanilla contrastive learning are identified: 1) Large intra-domain connectivity where datapoints within each domain forms clusters 2) Small intra-class connectivity where different classes are indistinguishable.

The paper leverage strong augmentations to reduce intra-domain connectivity. In order to increase the intra-class connectivity, the paper proposes CD2NN search strategy to find cross-domain matches and use them in the CL as positive pairs. The proposed CD2NN uses in-domain NN as a proxy to find more accurate cross domain neighbors.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1) Compared to UDA, UDG is more data efficient since it does not require a large labeled source dataset. 

2) The manuscript identify the main issues with using the vanilla CL approach for UDG.

3) The proposed CD2NN method is novel and helps in finding better cross domain matches according to the experiments. 


Weaknesses:

1) I wonder where UDG could be used in practice? Is it not more efficient to collect more data in the target dataset instead of using data from different domains? Unlabeled data collection is practical in many applications and could be easier than using UDG approach.

2) Intuitively, I understand what intra-domain and intra-class connectivity means. I also understand the definition of C_a and C_b in Equation 3.  Unfortunately, the paper does not provide an intuition why C_a (C_b) is related to intra-domain (intra-class) connectivity.

3) Proposition 1 states that stronger augmentation can decrease intra-domain connectivity which makes sense. However, the paper does not discuss the effect of stronger augmentation to intra-class connectivity. Intuitively, stronger augmentation should reduce both not only C_a.

4) The term "more accurate" in Proposal 3 is informal and vague. The reader should be able to understand the statement without reading the proof.

5) Some of the terms are used before definition. For instance, terms "intra-domain" and "intra-class" connectivity used in the abstract are not well defined until the end of page one. Another example is the reference to Fig 1 (in page 1) but reader can not fully understand the figure before reading "Vanilla contrastive learning (CL) fails in UDG." subsection.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper studies a new problem of UDG and identifies major issues with vanilla CL approach in this setting. Except for the issues mentioned above the paper was mostly clearly written. The experiments are explained in details and looks reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is well written and introduce a more data efficient DA approach. The proposed CD2NN seems to be an efficient way to help increase the intra-class connectivity. I hope the authors can address my concerns listed the weaknesses section above.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Because domain generalization work requires a large amount of labeled source data, this paper is committed to solving the problem by studying unsupervised domain generalization (UDG), and proposes a new contrastive learning method based on the problem that traditional contrastive learning is difficult to play in cross domain. The authors use data augmentation to suppress intra-domain connectivity and search for similar samples within and cross domains to enhance intra-class connectivity. This method has achieved the state-of-the-art in multiple experiments.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1.	The authors provide sufficient technical details for readers to understand the proposed techniques.
2.	The authors reveal that suppressing the intra-domain connectivity and encouraging the intra-class connectivity help to learn the domain-invariant semantic information. Such observation is helpful for UDG.
3.	The scheme for selecting samples is very creative and practical. Two schemes, cross-domain and intra-domain, are designed, and the model can take both benefits from them.
Weakness：
1.	Missing lots of details.
a)	How the model is trained? The authors just provide the reference of UDG and the reader must read the reference to understand what is the definition of UDG. Actually, UDG is not appropriate since a small labeled data is required to train a model. It is not totally unsupervised.
b)	There is no introduction to what the baseline is, please introduce which model has been improved in the ablation study.
2.	According to the visualization results of the model in Figure 8, the selected nearest neighbors are mostly from the same domain. It is difficult to believe that the model can learn enough good domain-independent features to achieve the SOTA.
3.	Data augmentation methods such as Rotate, Contrast, Color, and Sharpness are not enough to eliminate domain information and limit intra-domain connectivity. It is recommended to consider data augmentation methods related to style transfer.
4.	Minor: The bold numbers are not demonstrated. Do they just indicate the performances of the proposed method? You can just add a horizontal line above Ours (KNN) like the upper part in Table 2. By the way, such lines are missed in the middle and bottom parts in Table 2. Usually bold number indicates the best performance and the underlined number indicated the second best.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The organization of the paper should be improved especially for the setting of UDG and the training procedure. The novelty of this work is enough.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please see the Strength and Weakness.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper points out that semantic connectivity is the key to UDG. The authors proposed a UDG method, called DN2A to suppress the intra-domain connectivity and propose a novel dual nearest neighbor’s search strategy to find trustworthy cross domain neighbors to encourage the intra-class connectivity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1, The experimental results are promising. 
2, The motivation is clear. 


Weaknesses. 
About method and experiments: 
1, In Table 4, the baseline method achieves 36.42% accuracy, whereas the backbone in Table 1 (ERM) shows 13.82%. The backbone of the authors’ method is higher than most existing methods. It is not clear about the effectiveness of the proposed method. Is it due to the design of the methodology or a strong baseline? 
2, CD2NN aims to find the most trustworthy samples from cross domains as a positive sample to enlarge the intra-class connectivity. It is a bit tricky to decide when to find cross-domain nearest neighbors because the accurate positive pairs depend on a good network weight. How \lambda is changed according to the training epochs? 
 About the setting: 	
3, The authors aim to solve the unsupervised DG, where a pre-trained model and class label are not required, but a domain label is needed. I noticed the results obtained by the authors’ method are slightly higher than ImageNet initialization. 
4, I wonder if it is necessary to design an unsupervised method for DG without a pre-trained model. Many methods reported the pre-trained model for DG. If the authors use the pre-trained model, will the proposed methods still work well? I feel this paper is only meaningful if the proposed method still works well with pre-trained model. 
5, Recently, a lot of research has been done on pre-trained models for DG. The differences and advantages of the proposed setting should be highlighted. 
• About writing: 
6, The paper is not easy to read. The authors did not formulate the main idea in a good way.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents an interesting idea for unsupervised DG. The main idea is to find trustworthy positive samples from other domains. The overall performance is excellent. I have some concerns regarding the experimental settings. The authors may demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach with pre-trained models.
